☛ How many elements are there in the modern periodic table? → 118
☛ What property uniquely identifies an element? → Atomic number (number of protons)
☛ What are variants of an element with different neutron numbers called? → Isotopes
☛ Which element has the atomic number 1? → Hydrogen (H)

qs.tag: RRB JE ME 19 Sep 2019 Shift 2 CBT 2
q: Rutherford's alpha particle scattering experiment was responsible for the discovery of -
qs.e: Rutherford's alpha particle scattering experiment (1911) involved bombarding a thin gold foil with alpha particles (He²⁺ nuclei). Most particles passed through, but some were deflected at large angles, and a few bounced back. This observation contradicted the Thomson's plum pudding model and led Rutherford to propose that atoms have a tiny, dense, positively charged atomic nucleus at their center, where most mass is concentrated. The experiment did not discover the neutron (found by Chadwick in 1932), electron (discovered by J.J. Thomson in 1897), or proton (identified by Rutherford later, but the nucleus discovery was key).
qs.kf:
☛ Alpha particles are helium nuclei (He²⁺) with 2 protons and 2 neutrons.
☛ Rutherford's model suggested electrons orbit the nucleus, similar to planets around the sun.
☛ The nuclear model explained why most alpha particles passed through (empty space) and few were deflected (close to dense nucleus).
☛ This experiment led to the concept of the nuclear atom, fundamental to modern atomic theory.
☛ Later, Niels Bohr improved this model by quantizing electron orbits. Important One-liners for Upcoming Exams:
☛ Who discovered the atomic nucleus? → Ernest Rutherford
☛ Which experiment led to the discovery of the atomic nucleus? → Alpha particle scattering experiment
☛ What are alpha particles? → Helium nuclei (He²⁺)
☛ Which atomic model did Rutherford's experiment disprove? → Thomson's plum pudding model
☛ What did most alpha particles do in Rutherford's experiment? → Passed straight through the gold foil

qs.tag: RPF Constable 2024 : 12 Mar, 2025 Shift 1
q: The radioactive elements radium and polonium were discovered by:
qs.e: The discovery of radium and polonium was made by Marie Curie and her husband Pierre Curie in 1898. They isolated these elements from pitchblende ore through meticulous chemical separation techniques. Radium (atomic number 88) and polonium (atomic number 84) were the first radioactive elements discovered after uranium. Marie Curie coined the term "radioactivity" and received Nobel Prizes in both Physics (1903) and Chemistry (1911) for her work. Option 1 (John Dalton) proposed atomic theory but didn't discover these elements. Option 2 (Irène Joliot-Curie) was Marie's daughter who discovered artificial radioactivity later. Option 4 (Avogadro) proposed Avogadro's law for gases.
qs.kf:
☛ Marie Curie was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize and the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences
☛ Polonium was named after Marie Curie's native Poland
☛ Radium glows with a faint blue light due to its radioactivity
☛ The unit of radioactivity Curie (Ci) is named after Marie Curie
☛ Pitchblende is a uranium-rich mineral ore (mainly U₃O₈) Important One-liners for Upcoming Exams:
☛ Who discovered radium and polonium? → Marie Curie
☛ Which radioactive element is named after Poland? → Polonium
☛ Who coined the term 'radioactivity'? → Marie Curie
☛ What is the atomic number of radium? → 88
☛ From which ore were radium and polonium isolated? → Pitchblende

qs.tag: RRB JE CBT-2 2024 CMA : 22 Apr, 2025 Shift 1
q: Which of the following is a close packed plane for the HCP crystal?
qs.e: In Hexagonal Close-Packed (HCP) crystal structure, the close-packed planes are those with the highest atomic density. The Miller indices (hkil) notation is used for hexagonal systems. For HCP, the basal plane (0001) is the close-packed plane where atoms are arranged in a hexagonal pattern with maximum packing efficiency. This plane corresponds to the top and bottom faces of the hexagonal unit cell. Options (1011), (1010), and (1101) represent other crystallographic planes in HCP but are not close-packed. Specifically, (1010) is a prismatic plane, (1011) and (1101) are pyramidal planes, all having lower atomic density compared to the basal plane. The close-packed nature of (0001) is due to the ABAB... stacking sequence in HCP, where each atom contacts six neighbors in this plane.
qs.kf:
☛ HCP structure has a coordination number of 12 and examples include Mg, Zn, and Cd.
☛ The basal plane (0001) in HCP is perpendicular to the c-axis of the hexagonal unit cell.
☛ Miller indices are used to denote crystal planes and directions in all crystal systems.
☛ Close-packed structures include HCP and FCC (Face-Centered Cubic), both with 74% packing efficiency.
☛ In HCP, the stacking sequence is ABAB..., while in FCC it is ABCABC... Important One-liners for Upcoming Exams:
☛ What is the coordination number of HCP structure? → 12
☛ Which plane is close-packed in FCC crystal? → (111)
☛ What is the atomic packing factor of HCP? → 0.74
☛ Give an example of HCP metal. → Magnesium (Mg)
☛ What is the stacking sequence in HCP? → ABAB...

qs.tag: RRB ALP CBT-I 2024 : 28 Nov, 2024 Shift 3
q: What determines the chemical properties of a carbon compound?
qs.e: The functional group determines the chemical properties of a carbon compound because it is the reactive part of the molecule that undergoes specific chemical reactions. In organic chemistry, compounds with the same functional group exhibit similar chemical behavior regardless of the size of the carbon chain. For example, all alcohols contain the -OH group and undergo reactions like oxidation and esterification. Option 2 (Molecular mass) affects physical properties like boiling point but not chemical reactivity. Option 3 (Number of Hydrogen atoms) varies with structure but doesn't define reactivity patterns. Option 4 (Length of the carbon chain) influences physical properties and some reactivity trends, but the core chemical behavior is governed by the functional group.
qs.kf:
☛ Functional groups are specific arrangements of atoms that determine characteristic reactions of organic compounds.
☛ Homologous series are families of compounds with the same functional group but varying carbon chain lengths.
☛ Isomers can have different functional groups (functional group isomers) leading to completely different chemical properties.
☛ The IUPAC nomenclature system prioritizes functional groups when naming organic compounds.
☛ Compounds with multiple functional groups (polyfunctional) show combined reactivity patterns. Important One-liners for Upcoming Exams:
☛ What determines chemical properties in organic compounds? → Functional group
☛ Which part of an alcohol molecule makes it reactive? → Hydroxyl (-OH) group
☛ Do all carboxylic acids undergo similar reactions? → Yes, due to - COOH group
☛ What creates a homologous series? → Same functional group, differing by CH₂ units
☛ Can compounds with same molecular formula have different properties? → Yes, as functional group isomers

q: What does the formula Na 2 SO 4 indicate about the molecule?
qs.e: The chemical formula Na 2 SO 4 represents sodium sulfate, an ionic compound. In chemical formulas, subscript numbers indicate the number of atoms of each element present in one formula unit. Here, the subscript "2" after Na (sodium) means there are two sodium atoms. The formula shows: 2 sodium (Na) atoms, 1 sulfur (S) atom (no subscript means 1), and 4 oxygen (O) atoms. Option 1 is correct because it accurately states the sodium count. Option 2 is wrong as there are four oxygen atoms, not two. Option 3 is incorrect because there is only one sulfur atom. Option 4 is false as there are two sodium atoms, not four.
qs.kf:
☛ Na 2 SO 4 is commonly known as Glauber's salt when hydrated (Na 2 SO 4 ·10H 2 O).
☛ Sodium sulfate is used in detergents, paper manufacturing, and glass production.
☛ The sulfate ion (SO 4 2−) has a tetrahedral molecular geometry.
☛ In Na 2 SO 4, sodium has an oxidation state of +1 and sulfur has +6.
☛ This compound dissociates completely in water to form Na + and SO 4 2− ions. Important One-liners for Upcoming Exams:
☛ What is the common name of Na 2 SO 4 ·10H 2 O? → Glauber's salt
☛ How many oxygen atoms are in one formula unit of Na 2 SO 4 ? → Four
☛ What is the valency of sulfate ion in Na 2 SO 4 ? → 2-
☛ Na 2 SO 4 is an example of which type of compound? → Ionic salt
☛ What is the oxidation state of sulfur in Na 2 SO 4 ? → +6

qs.tag: RRB JE CBT 2 Electronics Engineering ReExam : 04 Jun, 2025
q: A student calculates the formula unit mass of calcium fluoride (CaF 2). If the atomic masses of Ca and F are 40 u and 19 u, respectively, what is the correct formula unit mass?
qs.e: The formula unit mass is calculated by summing the atomic masses of all atoms in the chemical formula. For calcium fluoride (CaF 2), the formula indicates one calcium atom and two fluorine atoms. Given atomic masses: Ca = 40 u, F = 19 u. Calculation: (1 × 40 u) + (2 × 19 u) = 40 u + 38 u = 78 u. Option 1 (97 u) is incorrect as it adds 40 + 19 + 19 incorrectly. Option 3 (100 u) is wrong—it might result from miscalculating 40 + (2 × 30). Option 4 (59 u) is incorrect, possibly from adding 40 + 19 only, ignoring the second fluorine atom. Thus, 78 u is correct.
qs.kf:
☛ Calcium fluoride (CaF 2) is an ionic compound, also known as fluorite.
☛ The atomic mass unit (u) is a standard unit for expressing atomic and molecular masses.
☛ In CaF 2, calcium has a valency of +2 and fluorine has -1, forming an ionic bond.
☛ Formula unit mass is used for ionic compounds, while molecular mass is for covalent compounds.
☛ The molar mass of CaF 2 is 78.07 g/mol, closely matching 78 u when rounded. Important One-liners for Upcoming Exams:
☛ What is the formula unit mass of NaCl if Na=23 u and Cl=35.5 u? → 58.5 u
☛ How is formula unit mass calculated? → Sum of atomic masses of all atoms in the formula
☛ What is the valency of calcium in CaF 2 ? → +2
☛ Is CaF 2 ionic or covalent? → Ionic
☛ What is the atomic mass unit based on? → 1/12 mass of carbon-12 atom

qs.tag: RRB JE CBT-I 2024 17 Dec 2024 Shift 1
q: Which of the following statements is true for a balanced chemical equation?
o: The total mass of molecules is unequal on both sides.
The total number of molecules is the same on both sides.
The total number of moles is the same on both sides.
The total number of atoms of each element is the same on both sides.
qs.e: A balanced chemical equation follows the Law of Conservation of Mass, which states that mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. This means the total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products. To satisfy this law, the number of atoms of each element must be equal on both sides of the equation, achieved by adjusting coefficients. Option 1 is incorrect because mass is conserved (equal on both sides). Option 2 is wrong as the number of molecules can differ (e.g., 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O has 3 reactant molecules and 2 product molecules). Option 3 is false because moles are not necessarily equal (e.g., in 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, there are 3 moles of reactants and 2 moles of products). Only Option 4 correctly describes atom conservation, ensuring mass balance.
qs.kf:
☛ Balancing equations involves adjusting coefficients, not subscripts, to maintain atom counts.
☛ The Law of Conservation of Mass was formulated by Antoine Lavoisier in the 18th century.
☛ In nuclear reactions, mass is not conserved due to mass-energy equivalence (E=mc²), but this does not apply to chemical reactions.
☛ A balanced equation provides the stoichiometric ratios for reactants and products.
☛ Unbalanced equations violate chemical principles and cannot predict reaction yields accurately. Important One-liners for Upcoming Exams:
☛ What does a balanced chemical equation obey? → Law of Conservation of Mass
☛ Who proposed the Law of Conservation of Mass? → Antoine Lavoisier
☛ In balancing, what do we adjust? → Coefficients, not subscripts
☛ What remains equal in a balanced equation? → Atoms of each element on both sides
☛ Can the number of molecules be different in a balanced equation? → Yes

q: What does the size of an atom mainly depend on?
o: Distance of electrons from the nucleus
qs.e: The size of an atom is primarily determined by the distance of the outermost electrons from the nucleus, which is influenced by the number of protons in the nucleus. According to Coulomb's Law, protons in the nucleus exert an attractive force on electrons. As the number of protons (atomic number) increases, the nuclear charge increases, pulling electrons closer to the nucleus, thereby decreasing atomic size across a period in the periodic table. Option 1 (Number of neutrons) is incorrect because neutrons affect atomic mass but not size directly. Option 3 (Number of isotopes) is wrong as isotopes have the same atomic number and similar size. Option 4 (Distance of electrons from the nucleus) describes the size itself, not what it depends on.
qs.kf:
☛ Atomic radius decreases across a period (left to right) due to increasing nuclear charge.
☛ Atomic radius increases down a group due to addition of new electron shells.
☛ Van der Waals radius is larger than covalent radius for the same atom.
☛ Ionic radius of cations is smaller than their atomic radius, while anions are larger.
☛ The smallest atom is Helium (He), and the largest naturally occurring atom is Francium (Fr). Important One-liners for Upcoming Exams:
☛ Atomic size decreases across a period due to? → Increase in nuclear charge
☛ Which has the smallest atomic radius? → Helium (He)
☛ Atomic size increases down a group because? → Addition of new electron shells
☛ Cations are smaller than their parent atoms because? → Loss of electrons reduces electron-electron repulsion
☛ Anions are larger than their parent atoms because? → Gain of electrons increases electron-electron repulsion

qs.tag: RRB Level 01 Stage I 24/12/2025 4:30 PM - 6:00 PM
q: The combining capacity of an element to each other primarily depends on which of the following?
qs.e: The combining capacity of an element, known as its valency, primarily depends on the number of valence electrons in its outermost shell. Valence electrons are involved in chemical bonding as atoms tend to achieve a stable electron configuration (usually an octet for main group elements). For example, sodium (Na) has 1 valence electron and loses it to form Na⁺ with valency 1, while chlorine (Cl) has 7 valence electrons and gains 1 electron to form Cl⁻ with valency 1. Option 1 (number of protons) determines the atomic number and element identity but not directly valency. Option 2 (number of energy levels) affects atomic size and ionization energy but not primary combining capacity. Option 4 (number of neutrons) influences isotopic mass and nuclear stability but does not affect chemical bonding.
qs.kf:
☛ Valence electrons are electrons in the outermost shell (highest principal quantum number) of an atom.
☛ Elements in the same group of the periodic table have the same number of valence electrons and similar chemical properties.
☛ Noble gases (Group 18) have a complete octet (except helium with 2 electrons) and are chemically inert due to stable valence electron configuration.
☛ Valency can be variable for transition elements due to involvement of d-electrons in bonding.
☛ The octet rule states that atoms tend to combine in such a way that each atom has eight electrons in its valence shell. Important One-liners for Upcoming Exams:
☛ What determines the chemical properties of an element? → Number of valence electrons
☛ Which electrons participate in bond formation? → Valence electrons
☛ Why do elements in the same group show similar chemical behavior? → Same number of valence electrons
☛ What is the valency of an element with 4 valence electrons? → Usually 4 (e.g., carbon in Group 14)
☛ Which group elements have zero valency? → Noble gases (Group 18)

qs.tag: RRB ALP CBT-I 2024 : 25 Nov, 2024 Shift 2
q: Which of the following options represents sub-atomic particles found in Thomson’s model of an atom?
qs.e: J.J. Thomson's Plum Pudding Model (1897) proposed that an atom consists of a uniform positively charged sphere with negatively charged electrons embedded in it, like plums in a pudding. This model was based on his cathode ray experiments, which discovered electrons as subatomic particles. Protons were discovered later by Ernest Rutherford (1911) through his gold foil experiment, and neutrons were discovered by James Chadwick in 1932. Therefore, Thomson's model only included electrons as subatomic particles. Option 2 is incorrect because neutrons were unknown. Option 3 is wrong as protons were not part of this model. Option 4 is incorrect since protons were not included; the positive charge was considered a continuous sphere.
qs.kf:
☛ Thomson discovered electrons using cathode ray tubes and determined their charge-to-mass ratio (e/m).
☛ The Plum Pudding Model was the first to incorporate subatomic particles, challenging Dalton's indivisible atom theory.
☛ Thomson's model could not explain Rutherford's alpha particle scattering results, leading to the nuclear model.
☛ In this model, the atom is electrically neutral because the total negative charge of electrons equals the positive charge of the sphere.
☛ Thomson received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1906 for his work on electrical conductivity in gases. Important One-liners for Upcoming Exams:
☛ Who discovered the electron? → J.J. Thomson
☛ What is Thomson's atomic model called? → Plum Pudding Model
☛ Which subatomic particle is present in Thomson's model? → Only electrons
☛ Which experiment led to the discovery of electrons? → Cathode ray experiment
☛ What was the main limitation of Thomson's model? → It could not explain Rutherford's scattering results

qs.tag: RRB Level 01 Stage I 10/02/2026 9:00 AM - 10:30 AM
q: Which of the following statements about a proton is correct ?
o: A proton is negatively charged and has very small mass
A proton is positively charged and its mass is taken as one unit
A proton is positively charged and mass is 1/2000 of a hydrogen atom
A proton is neutral in charge and has mass equal to an electron
qs.e: According to atomic structure, a proton is a subatomic particle found in the nucleus of an atom. It carries a positive charge of +1 elementary charge (approximately 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C). The mass of a proton is approximately 1 atomic mass unit (amu) or 1.6726 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, which is taken as the standard unit for atomic mass. Option 1 is incorrect because protons are positively charged, not negatively charged. Option 3 is incorrect because the mass of a proton is approximately equal to that of a hydrogen atom (since hydrogen's nucleus contains only one proton), not 1/2000 of it (that describes an electron's mass relative to a proton). Option 4 is incorrect because protons are not neutral—they are positively charged —and their mass is about 1836 times that of an electron, not equal.
qs.kf:
☛ Protons are discovered by Ernest Rutherford in his gold foil experiment (1911).
☛ The number of protons in an atom's nucleus defines its atomic number (Z), which determines the chemical element.
☛ In a neutral atom, the number of protons equals the number of electrons.
☛ Protons are composed of quarks (two up quarks and one down quark) held together by the strong nuclear force.
☛ The mass of a proton is approximately 1 amu, while the mass of a neutron is slightly more (about 1.0087 amu). Important One-liners for Upcoming Exams:
☛ Who discovered the proton? → Ernest Rutherford
☛ What is the charge of a proton? → Positive (+1)
☛ What is the approximate mass of a proton in atomic mass units? → 1 amu
☛ Which subatomic particle determines the atomic number of an element? → Proton
☛ How does the mass of a proton compare to that of an electron? → Proton is about 1836 times heavier

qs.tag: RPF SI Previous Paper : 6 Jan 2019 Shift 2
q: Which is called as the percentage of space occupied by constituent particles packed inside the lattice?
qs.e: In crystal structures, packing efficiency is defined as the percentage of total space occupied by constituent particles (atoms, ions, or molecules) within a unit cell. It's calculated using the formula: Packing Efficiency = (Volume occupied by particles in unit cell / Total volume of unit cell) × 100%. Different crystal structures have characteristic packing efficiencies: simple cubic (52.4%), body-centered cubic (68%), and face-centered cubic/hexagonal close-packed (74%). Options 2-4 are incorrect: Structural Functionality refers to how structure relates to properties, Laty Functionality is not a standard term in crystallography, and Solid Functionality describes practical applications of solid materials rather than spatial arrangement.

☛ Packing efficiency helps determine density of crystalline solids
☛ Close-packed structures (FCC and HCP) have the highest packing efficiency (74%)
☛ Void spaces in crystal lattices are called interstitial sites
☛ Coordination number indicates how many nearest neighbors each particle has
☛ Atomic packing factor is another name for packing efficiency in metallurgy Important One-liners for Upcoming Exams:
☛ What is the packing efficiency of simple cubic structure? → 52.4%
☛ Which crystal structure has maximum packing efficiency? → FCC and HCP (74%)
☛ What percentage of space is empty in BCC structure? → 32%

qs.tag: RRB Level 01 Stage I 14/12/2025 4:30 PM - 6:00 PM
q: Which of the following statements is correct about the concept of 'molecules of compounds'?
o: A molecule of a compound is formed by the combination of atoms of different elements.
A molecule of a compound is formed by the separation of atoms of different elements.
A molecule of a compound is formed by the combination of atoms of the same element.
A molecule of a compound is formed by the separation of atoms of the same element.
qs.e: According to the Law of Definite Proportions and basic chemical bonding principles, a compound is a substance formed when atoms of two or more different elements combine chemically in a fixed ratio. Therefore, a molecule of a compound consists of atoms of different elements bonded together. For example, a water molecule (H₂O) contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. Option 1 is correct because it accurately describes this fundamental concept. Option 2 is incorrect because compounds form through combination, not separation. Option 3 describes a molecule of an element (like O₂ or N₂), not a compound. Option 4 is also wrong as separation of same-element atoms doesn't create compounds.
qs.kf:
☛ Compounds have properties different from their constituent elements (e.g., NaCl is salty while Na is reactive metal and Cl₂ is toxic gas).
☛ The smallest unit of a compound that retains its chemical properties is called a molecule.
☛ Chemical bonds (ionic, covalent, or metallic) hold atoms together in compounds.
☛ Compounds can be represented by chemical formulas showing element symbols and atom ratios (e.g., CO₂ for carbon dioxide).
☛ Elements form molecules too (e.g., O₂, H₂) but these are not compounds. Important One-liners for Upcoming Exams:
☛ What is a molecule of a compound? → Smallest unit of a compound with atoms of different elements chemically bonded.
☛ How do compounds differ from elements? → Compounds contain atoms of different elements; elements contain same-type atoms.
☛ What law governs compound formation? → Law of Definite Proportions (constant composition).
☛ Give an example of a compound molecule. → H₂O (water) with H and O atoms.
☛ Can same-element atoms form compounds? → No, they form molecules of elements (e.g., O₂).

qs.tag: RRB NTPC CBT-I : 3 April 2021 Shift 1
q: The term ‘Isotope’ refers to:-
o: elements having same atomic number but different mass number
elements having different atomic number but same mass number
elements having same physical and chemical properties
qs.e: The term isotope refers to atoms of the same element that have identical atomic numbers (number of protons) but different mass numbers (sum of protons and neutrons). This occurs because isotopes contain different numbers of neutrons in their nuclei while maintaining the same number of protons. For example, Carbon-12 (6 protons, 6 neutrons) and Carbon-14 (6 protons, 8 neutrons) are isotopes of carbon. Option 1 is incorrect because bond structure relates to molecular arrangement, not atomic identity. Option 3 describes isobars (elements with same mass number but different atomic numbers). Option 4 is wrong because isotopes have similar chemical properties but often different physical properties (like density or radioactivity) due to mass differences.
qs.kf:
☛ Isotopes of an element occupy same position in periodic table due to identical atomic numbers
☛ Chemical properties depend on electron configuration, which is same for isotopes
☛ Physical properties like density, boiling point, and nuclear stability vary among isotopes
☛ Some isotopes are radioactive (e.g., Carbon-14) while others are stable (e.g., Carbon-12)
☛ Mass spectrometry is used to separate and identify different isotopes Important One-liners for Upcoming Exams:

☛ Isotopes differ in which particles? → Number of neutrons
☛ Do isotopes have same chemical properties? → Yes, due to identical electron configuration
☛ What are isobars? → Atoms with same mass number but different atomic numbers

q: Rutherford’s α-particle scattering experiment led to the discovery of which of the following?

The experiment did not discover protons (identified later by Rutherford in 1917), neutrons (discovered by Chadwick in 1932), or electrons (discovered by J.J. Thomson in 1897).

qs.tag: RPF Constable 2018 12 Feb 2019
q: Which of the following is a triatomic molecule?
qs.e: A triatomic molecule contains exactly three atoms. Ozone (O₃) consists of three oxygen atoms bonded together, making it triatomic. Hydrogen (H₂) is diatomic with two hydrogen atoms. Helium (He) and Neon (Ne) are noble gases that exist as monatomic molecules (single atoms) under standard conditions. Helium has atomic number 2 and neon has atomic number 10; both are chemically inert and do not form diatomic or triatomic molecules naturally. The correct option is ozone because its molecular formula O₃ confirms three atoms. The wrong options are incorrect: hydrogen has two atoms, while helium and neon are single atoms.

☛ Ozone (O₃) is an allotrope of oxygen, with a bent molecular shape and bond angle of about 116.8°.
☛ Noble gases like helium, neon, argon are monatomic due to complete valence shells (octet or duplet).
☛ Common diatomic molecules include H₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂ (remember as HOFBrINCl).
☛ Atomicity refers to the number of atoms in a molecule: monatomic (1), diatomic (2), triatomic (3), polyatomic (>3).
☛ Phosphorus (P₄) is a tetratomic molecule, and sulfur (S₈) is octatomic at room temperature. Important One-liners for Upcoming Exams:

☛ What is the atomicity of helium? → Monatomic (1)
☛ Name a diatomic noble gas? → None; all noble gases are monatomic
☛ How many atoms are in an ozone molecule? → Three
☛ Which is not a diatomic molecule: O₂ or Ne? → Ne (neon is monatomic)

qs.tag: RRB JE 27 May 2019 Shift 1 CBT 1
q: The number of atoms or molecules or ions present in one mole of a substance is called-
qs.e: The number of atoms, molecules, or ions present in one mole of any substance is called the Avogadro number (N A). This fundamental constant has a fixed value of approximately 6.022 × 10 23 entities per mole. It is named after the Italian scientist Amedeo Avogadro and is crucial in relating macroscopic measurements to microscopic particles. Option 1 (Normality) is incorrect because it refers to the gram-equivalent concentration of a solution. Option 3 (Mass number) is wrong as it denotes the total number of protons and neutrons in an atom's nucleus. Option 4 (Atomic number) is incorrect since it represents the number of protons in an atom's nucleus, which determines the element's identity.
qs.kf:
☛ The Avogadro number is defined as the number of atoms in exactly 12 grams of carbon-12 isotope.
☛ One mole of any gas at STP (Standard Temperature and Pressure) occupies 22.4 liters volume.
☛ The molar mass of a substance (in grams per mole) numerically equals its atomic/molecular mass.
☛ Avogadro's Law states that equal volumes of all gases at same temperature and pressure contain equal number of molecules.
☛ The concept of mole connects microscopic particles to measurable macroscopic quantities in chemistry. Important One-liners for Upcoming Exams:
☛ What is the value of Avogadro number? → 6.022 × 10 23

qs.e: In nuclear chemistry, nuclides are classified based on their atomic number (Z) and mass number (A). Nuclides with the same mass number but different atomic numbers are called isobars. For example, ⁴⁰₁₈Ar and ⁴⁰₂₀Ca both have mass number 40 but different atomic numbers (18 and 20). Isotones (Option 1) have the same number of neutrons but different atomic numbers. qs.tag: RRB JE 29 May 2019 Shift 2 CBT 1
q: The cathode ray experiment was done for the first time by-
qs.e: The cathode ray experiment was first conducted by J.J. Thomson in 1897. This experiment involved passing an electric current through a gas at low pressure in a cathode ray tube. Thomson observed that cathode rays traveled from the cathode to the anode and could be deflected by electric and magnetic fields, indicating they were composed of negatively charged particles. He measured the charge-to-mass ratio (e/m) of these particles, which were later named electrons. This discovery proved that atoms are divisible and contain subatomic particles. Option 2 (Ernest Rutherford) is incorrect because he conducted the gold foil experiment in 1911, discovering the nucleus. Option 3 (John Dalton) proposed the atomic theory in 1808 but did not perform cathode ray experiments. Option 4 (Goldstein) discovered protons in 1886 using a modified cathode ray tube, but Thomson's work came later and was more foundational for electron discovery.

q: Which of the following scientists gave the concept of atomic mass?
qs.e: The concept of atomic mass was introduced by John Dalton in his Atomic Theory (1808). He developed the first table of relative atomic weights (now called atomic masses) by comparing elements to hydrogen as the standard. Ernest Rutherford discovered the atomic nucleus (1911), J.J. Thomson discovered the electron (1897), and Niels Bohr proposed the quantum model of the atom (1913) — none introduced atomic mass. Dalton's work enabled stoichiometric calculations and the law of multiple proportions.

q: According to Rutherford's model of an atom, where is most of the mass of the atom located?
qs.e: According to Rutherford's nuclear model of the atom (1911), based on his gold foil experiment, most of the mass of an atom is concentrated in a tiny, dense, positively charged region called the nucleus. This conclusion came from observing that most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil, but a few were deflected at large angles or even bounced back, indicating a concentrated mass. The electrons revolve around the nucleus in circular paths, but they contribute negligible mass because an electron's mass (~9.1×10⁻³¹ kg) is about 1/1837 of a proton's mass. Option 1 is incorrect because electron shells contain electrons with very little mass. Option 3 is incorrect as the electron cloud is a quantum mechanical concept not part of Rutherford's model. Option 4 is incorrect because mass is not uniformly distributed; it's highly concentrated in the nucleus.
qs.kf:

☛ The nucleus contains protons and neutrons, collectively called nucleons.

q: A positively charged ion is called a/an:
qs.e: In atomic structure, an ion is an atom or molecule that has gained or lost one or more electrons, resulting in a net electric charge. A positively charged ion is formed when an atom loses one or more electrons, leaving it with more protons than electrons. This type of ion is specifically called a cation. The term "cation" originates from the Greek word "kata," meaning "down," as cations migrate toward the cathode (negative electrode) during electrolysis. Option 1 (molecule) is incorrect because a molecule is a neutral group of atoms bonded together. Option 2 (atom) is wrong as an atom is electrically neutral with equal protons and electrons. Option 3 (anion) is incorrect because an anion is a negatively charged ion formed by gaining electrons.
qs.kf:
☛ Cations are typically formed by metals (e.g., Na⁺, Ca²⁺, Al³⁺) due to their low ionization energies.
☛ The charge of a cation is indicated by a superscript plus sign (e.g., Mg²⁺ for magnesium ion).
☛ Anions are negatively charged ions formed by nonmetals gaining electrons (e.g., Cl⁻, O²⁻).

q: How much is the molar mass of nitrous acid (HNO 2)?
qs.e: The molar mass of a compound is calculated by summing the atomic masses of all atoms in its chemical formula. For nitrous acid (HNO₂), we use standard atomic masses: Hydrogen (H) = 1.008 g/mol, Nitrogen (N) = 14.007 g/mol, and Oxygen (O) = 15.999 g/mol. Calculation: H (1 × 1.008) + N (1 × 14.007) + O₂ (2 × 15.999) = 1.008 + 14.007 + 31.998 = 47.013 g/mol. Option 4 is correct as it matches this precise value. Option 1 (44.01 g/mol) is close to CO₂'s molar mass. Option 2 (63.01 g/mol) approximates HNO₃'s molar mass. Option 3 (36.46 g/mol) matches HCl's molar mass. All wrong options correspond to other common compounds.
qs.kf:
☛ Nitrous acid (HNO₂) is a weak acid and decomposes readily to form nitric oxide (NO) and nitric acid (HNO₃).
☛ The oxidation state of nitrogen in HNO₂ is +3, making it an intermediate in nitrogen redox reactions.
☛ Nitrous acid is used in the preparation of diazonium salts, important in dye and pharmaceutical industries.
☛ The conjugate base of nitrous acid is the nitrite ion (NO₂⁻), commonly found in preservatives.
☛ Molar mass is expressed in grams per mole (g/mol) and is numerically equal to molecular weight in atomic mass units (amu). Important One-liners for Upcoming Exams:

q: What does the subscript in a chemical formula represent?
o: The oxidation state of the element
The number of atoms of each element in a molecule
qs.e: In chemical formulas, the subscript (small number written below and to the right of an element symbol) indicates the number of atoms of that element present in one molecule of the compound. For example, in H₂O, the subscript '2' shows there are two hydrogen atoms, and the implied subscript '1' for oxygen shows one oxygen atom. This follows the standard chemical notation rules established by IUPAC. Option 1 is incorrect because oxidation state is shown by superscript with charge sign (e.g., Fe³⁺). Option 2 is wrong as mass is calculated from atomic masses, not directly from subscripts. Option 4 is incorrect since ionic charge is also indicated by superscript (e.g., SO₄²⁻).

qs.tag: RRB NTPC GRADUATE CBT 1 25/03/2026 4:30 PM - 6:00 PM
q: Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden performed the famous α–particle scattering experiment under the supervision of _________.
qs.e: The famous α-particle scattering experiment (also known as the Geiger-Marsden experiment or gold foil experiment) was conducted by Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden in 1909 under the direct supervision of Ernest Rutherford at the University of Manchester. This experiment involved bombarding a thin gold foil with α-particles (helium nuclei, He²⁺) from a radioactive source. Most α-particles passed straight through, but some were deflected at large angles, and a few even bounced back. Rutherford interpreted these surprising results to propose his nuclear model of the atom in 1911, where most of the atom's mass and positive charge are concentrated in a tiny, dense nucleus. Niels Bohr later refined this model with quantum theory (1913). John Dalton proposed the atomic theory in 1808, and William Henry formulated Henry's law for gas solubility in 1803—neither was involved in this experiment.
qs.kf:
☛ The α-particle scattering experiment led to the discovery of the atomic nucleus.
☛ Rutherford's model suggested that atoms are mostly empty space, with electrons orbiting a dense, positively charged nucleus.
☛ The experiment used a thin gold foil (about 1000 atoms thick) as the target material.
☛ About 1 in 8000 α-particles were deflected at angles greater than 90°, indicating a strong repulsive force from a concentrated positive charge.
☛ This experiment disproved J.J. Thomson's "plum pudding" model of the atom, which suggested a uniform distribution of positive charge. Important One-liners for Upcoming Exams:
☛ Who supervised the α-particle scattering experiment? → Ernest Rutherford
☛ What did the α-particle scattering experiment discover? → The atomic nucleus
☛ Who conducted the α-particle scattering experiment? → Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden
☛ Which model of the atom did the α-particle scattering experiment disprove? → J.J. Thomson's plum pudding model
☛ What particles were used in the Geiger-Marsden experiment? → α-particles (helium nuclei)

q: Which of the following statements about neutrons is correct?

They are found in the nucleus of an atom.
They revolve around the nucleus in fixed orbits.
qs.e: According to the Rutherford-Bohr atomic model, an atom consists of a central nucleus containing protons (positively charged) and neutrons (neutral), with electrons orbiting around it. Neutrons are subatomic particles with zero charge (neutral) and a mass of approximately 1.675 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, similar to protons. They are indeed found in the nucleus alongside protons. Option 1 is incorrect because neutrons have no charge, not positive. Option 2 is wrong as electrons, particularly valence electrons, determine chemical properties, not neutrons. Option 4 is false because electrons revolve around the nucleus, not neutrons.

q: If glucose :: six-carbon molecule, then pyruvate :: _______.
qs.e: This question tests knowledge of molecular structure in biochemistry. Glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆) is a six-carbon monosaccharide (hexose) that serves as a primary energy source in living organisms. During glycolysis, glucose is broken down into two molecules of pyruvate (CH₃COCOOH), which is a three-carbon compound. Pyruvate contains three carbon atoms in its structure, making it a key intermediate in cellular respiration. Option 1 (four-carbon) is incorrect because molecules like oxaloacetate have four carbons. Option 3 (five-carbon) describes compounds like ribose. Option 4 (two-carbon) refers to molecules like acetyl- CoA precursor. Thus, pyruvate is correctly identified as a three-carbon molecule.

q: According to Mendeleev's periodic law, the elements were arranged in the periodic table in the order of ________.

Option 1 is correct because Mendeleev specifically used atomic mass as the primary organizing principle. Option 2 (decreasing atomic masses) is incorrect as he arranged them in ascending order. q: The sum of the atomic masses of all the atoms in a molecule of the substance is -
qs.e: The sum of the atomic masses of all atoms in a molecule is called the molecular mass. It is calculated by adding the atomic masses (from the periodic table) of each atom in the molecular formula. For example, the molecular mass of water (H₂O) is (2 × 1.008) + (1 × 16.00) = 18.016 u. Formula mass refers to ionic compounds like NaCl, not covalent molecules. Mole is the amount of substance containing Avogadro's number of particles (6.022 × 10²³), not a mass sum. Atomic mass is the mass of a single atom, not the sum for a molecule. Thus, only molecular mass correctly describes the total atomic mass in a molecule.

q: Which of the following is NOT an isotope of hydrogen atom?

Helium (He) is a different element with atomic number 2, containing 2 protons in its nucleus. Since isotopes must belong to the same element, helium cannot be an isotope of hydrogen. Thus, option 2 is correct because it is not an isotope of hydrogen, while options 1, 3, and 4 are isotopes of hydrogen.

q: According to the sign convention, the height of an erect image formed by a mirror is taken as:

qs.tag: RRB NTPC UG CBT-I : 29 Aug, 2025 Shift 2
q: Which postulate of Dalton’s atomic theory explains the Law of Definite Proportions?
o: Atoms of different elements have different masses and properties.
Atoms of the same element are identical in mass and size.
Atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios to form compounds.
qs.e: The Law of Definite Proportions states that a chemical compound always contains exactly the same proportion of elements by mass. Dalton's atomic theory explains this through the postulate that atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios to form compounds. This means compounds are formed by fixed ratios of atoms (e.g., water H₂O always has 2 hydrogen atoms to 1 oxygen atom), leading to constant mass proportions. Option 1 describes atomic indivisibility (explaining conservation of mass in reactions). Option 2 explains differences between elements. Option 3 explains uniformity within an element (Law of Multiple Proportions partially). Only Option 4 directly accounts for the fixed atomic ratios in compounds, which mathematically yields definite mass proportions as per the law.

q: Which of the following statements is FALSE about mass number?
o: It represents total nucleons in the atom.
It is always a whole number.
It is equal to twice the atomic number for all elements.
It may differ for isotopes of the same element.
qs.e: The mass number (A) of an atom is defined as the total number of protons and neutrons (nucleons) in its nucleus. It is always a whole number because it counts discrete particles. For isotopes of the same element, which have the same atomic number (number of protons) but different numbers of neutrons, the mass number differs. However, the statement that mass number equals twice the atomic number for all elements is false. This would only be true if every atom had equal numbers of protons and neutrons, which is not the case. For example, in carbon-12 (atomic number 6, mass number 12), it holds true, but for uranium-238 (atomic number 92, mass number 238), it does not. Thus, option 3 is incorrect, while options 1, 2, and 4 are correct statements about mass number.

qs.tag: RRB Level 01 Stage I 11/12/2025 12:45 PM - 2:15 PM
q: Rutherford's gold foil experiment led to a major revision of the atomic model. Which of the following observations and conclusions is most accurate according to the experiment?
o: Electrons are present in the nucleus and account for the atom's mass.
Alpha particles are deflected because they collide with electrons and spread uniformly throughout the atom.
The nucleus is positively charged and occupies most of the volume of the atom.
The majority of alpha particles passed through the foil undeflected, indicating that atoms are mostly empty space.
qs.e: Rutherford's gold foil experiment involved bombarding a thin gold foil with alpha particles (α-particles, He²⁺ ions). Most α-particles passed straight through the foil without deflection, indicating that atoms are mostly empty space. A small fraction were deflected at large angles, and a very few bounced back, revealing a small, dense, positively charged nucleus. Option 1 is incorrect because electrons are outside the nucleus and have negligible mass; protons and neutrons account for atomic mass. Option 2 is wrong as α-particles are deflected by the positively charged nucleus, not electrons, and electrons do not cause uniform spreading. Option 3 is inaccurate because the nucleus occupies a very small volume (~10⁻¹⁵ m) compared to the atom (~10⁻¹⁰ m).

q: Electrons are fundamental particles that make up matter. Who among the following is credited with this discovery?
qs.e: The discovery of the electron as a fundamental particle of matter is credited to J.J. Thomson in 1897 through his cathode ray tube experiments. q: Which of the following is NOT a subatomic particle?
qs.e: In atomic structure, subatomic particles are the fundamental constituents that make up an atom. The three primary subatomic particles are the proton (positively charged, found in the nucleus), neutron (neutral, found in the nucleus), and electron (negatively charged, orbiting the nucleus). A molecule is not a subatomic particle; it is a group of two or more atoms chemically bonded together, representing the smallest unit of a compound that retains its chemical properties. Therefore, while options 1, 2, and 3 are subatomic particles, option 4 is incorrect because a molecule is a larger entity composed of multiple atoms, not a fundamental particle within an atom.

qs.tag: RRB NTPC Graduate Level CBT-I : 19 Jun, 2025 Shift 3
q: At STP, the number of molecules present in 5.6 L of O2 gas is:
qs.e: At STP (Standard Temperature and Pressure: 0°C and 1 atm), 1 mole of any ideal gas occupies 22.4 L volume (Molar Volume). Given volume of O₂ gas = 5.6 L. First, calculate number of moles: n = Volume / Molar Volume = 5.6 L / 22.4 L/mol = 0.25 mol. Each mole contains Avogadro's number of molecules (Nₐ = 6.022 × 10²³ molecules/mol). Thus, number of molecules = n × Nₐ = 0.25 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 1.5055 × 10²³ molecules. Option 1 (6.022 × 10²³) is incorrect because it represents molecules in 1 mole (22.4 L at STP), not 5.6 L. Option 3 (2.24 × 10²³) is wrong as it corresponds to 0.372 moles (≈8.33 L). Option 4 (3.011 × 10²³) is incorrect since it equals molecules in 0.5 moles (11.2 L at STP).
qs.kf:
☛ STP conditions are 0°C (273.15 K) and 1 atm pressure (101.325 kPa).
☛ Avogadro's Law states equal volumes of all gases at same temperature and pressure contain equal number of molecules.
☛ Molar volume at NTP (20°C, 1 atm) is 24.0 L/mol, different from STP.
☛ Oxygen (O₂) is a diatomic molecule; atomic mass of oxygen is 16 u, so molar mass of O₂ is 32 g/mol.

☛ Calculate number of moles in 44.8 L of N₂ at STP. → 2 moles

q: The atomic mass of an atom is primarily determined by the number of:
qs.e: The atomic mass of an atom is primarily determined by the total number of nucleons (protons + neutrons) in its nucleus. This is because electrons have negligible mass (approximately 1/1836 of a proton's mass), so their contribution to atomic mass is insignificant. Protons and neutrons each have a mass of approximately 1 atomic mass unit (amu), while electrons contribute only about 0.00055 amu. Therefore, the atomic mass is essentially the sum of protons and neutrons. Option 1 (electrons) is incorrect because electrons determine chemical properties and charge, not mass. Option 3 (protons) alone gives the atomic number, not mass. Option 4 (neutrons) affects isotopes but not the primary mass determination.

qs.e: The standard unit for measuring atomic or molecular scale masses is the unified atomic mass unit (u), also called dalton (Da). It is defined as 1/12th the mass of a carbon-12 atom. q: If two isotopes of an element ‘X’ are X-35 and X-37, the average atomic mass of chlorine (if X-35 = 25% and X-37 = 75%) will be:
qs.e: The average atomic mass of an element with multiple isotopes is calculated using the weighted average formula : Average atomic mass = (Fraction of isotope 1 × Mass of isotope 1) + (Fraction of isotope 2 × Mass of isotope 2). Here, isotope X-35 has mass 35 u and abundance 25% (0.25 fraction), while isotope X-37 has mass 37 u and abundance 75% (0.75 fraction). Calculation: (0.25 × 35) + (0.75 × 37) = 8.75 + 27.75 = 36.5 u. This matches option 4. Option 1 (35.5 u) is incorrect—it assumes equal abundances (50% each). Option 2 (36.0 u) is wrong as it uses a simple average. Option 3 (34.5 u) is erroneous due to incorrect subtraction or miscalculation.
qs.kf:

q: What is the characteristic of forming covalent bonds by carbon with another carbon atoms?
qs.e: The ability of carbon atoms to form covalent bonds with other carbon atoms, creating long chains or rings, is called catenation. This property arises because carbon has a small atomic size and high bond strength (C–C bond energy ~348 kJ/mol), allowing stable chains. Carbon's tetravalency (valency 4) enables it to form four covalent bonds via sp³, sp², or sp hybridization, leading to diverse structures like alkanes, alkenes, and aromatic compounds. Option 1 (Electronation) refers to gaining electrons, not chain formation. Option 2 (Ionization) involves forming ions, which carbon rarely does due to its high ionization energy. Option 3 (Electrolysis) is a process using electricity to drive non-spontaneous reactions, unrelated to carbon bonding.

☛ The ability to catenate allows carbon to form millions of organic compounds, including polymers like polyethylene and biomolecules like DNA.
☛ Carbon's tetravalency and hybridization (sp³, sp², sp) explain the geometry of its compounds, e.g., methane (tetrahedral) and ethene (trigonal planar).

The atomic radius is measured as the distance from the nucleus to the outermost electron shell. While the nucleus contains protons and neutrons that determine the atomic mass and charge, it does not directly define the atom's size. The nucleus itself is extremely small (~10⁻¹⁵ m) compared to the overall atom (~10⁻¹⁰ m). Therefore, option 1 is correct because electron clouds establish the boundary of the atom. Options 2 and 3 are incorrect as neutrons and protons only affect mass and nuclear properties, not size. Option 4 is incorrect because the nucleus is tiny and does not dictate the atom's dimensions.

q: What do members of a homologous series differ from each other by?

q: Why do covalently bonded compounds have low boiling point?
o: Have strong covalent bond within molecules but weak intermolecular force

However, the intermolecular forces (like van der Waals forces or dipole-dipole interactions) are weak. Boiling involves overcoming these intermolecular forces to separate molecules into the gaseous state, not breaking covalent bonds. Since these forces are weak, less energy (lower temperature) is needed, resulting in low boiling points. Option 2 is incorrect because covalent bonds are strong, not weak. Option 3 is wrong as strong intermolecular forces would lead to high boiling points. Option 4 is false because intermolecular forces are weak, not strong, and covalent bonds are strong.

Hydrogen bonding is a stronger intermolecular force that increases boiling points (e.g., in H₂O). Ionic compounds have high boiling points due to strong electrostatic forces between ions. Melting and boiling points depend on the strength of intermolecular forces, not covalent bond strength. Important One-liners for Upcoming Exams:

q: Who first proposed a law in 1931 to clarify the idea of thermal equilibrium and its significance in determining temperature?
qs.e: In 1931, Ralph H. Fowler proposed the Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics to clarify the concept of thermal equilibrium and its significance in temperature measurement. This law states: If two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third system, then they are in thermal equilibrium with each other. This establishes temperature as a fundamental property that determines the direction of heat flow and allows for consistent temperature measurement using thermometers. The other options are incorrect: Hugh L. Callendar worked on platinum resistance thermometers, James P. Espy was a meteorologist known for convection theories, and Rudolf Clausius formulated the Second Law of Thermodynamics and entropy concept. Fowler's formulation was crucial because it provided the logical foundation for temperature scales before the First and Second Laws were established.

☛ This law was named "Zeroth" because it was recognized as fundamental after the First and Second Laws had already been established.

q: Which of the following observations could NOT be explained by Rutherford’s model of the atom?
o: The presence of a positively charged nucleus in the atom
The distribution of electrons around the nucleus
The deflection of alpha particles at large angles
The stability of the atom despite the presence of accelerating electrons
qs.e: Rutherford's nuclear model (1911) proposed that an atom consists of a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus at the center, with electrons revolving around it in circular orbits. This model successfully explained: (1) The presence of a positively charged nucleus (from alpha-particle scattering experiments), (2) The distribution of electrons around the nucleus (as planetary orbits), and (3) The deflection of alpha particles at large angles (due to Coulombic repulsion from the nucleus). However, according to classical electromagnetic theory, an accelerating charged particle (like an electron in circular motion) should continuously emit radiation, lose energy, and spiral into the nucleus within ~10⁻⁸ seconds, making the atom unstable. Rutherford's model could NOT explain why atoms are stable despite this predicted collapse. This limitation was later addressed by Bohr's model (1913), which introduced quantized orbits.

q: Which sub-atomic particle was discovered by J Chadwick?
qs.e: The neutron was discovered by British physicist James Chadwick in 1932 through experiments involving beryllium bombardment with alpha particles (α-particles). q: If the object is placed between infinity and optical centre O of the concave lens, how will the image be formed after refraction?
qs.e: This question involves image formation by concave lenses using ray optics principles. For a concave (diverging) lens, when an object is placed anywhere between infinity and the optical centre (O), the image is always formed on the same side as the object, between the optical centre and the principal focus (F). The image characteristics are: virtual (cannot be projected on a screen), erect (upright), and diminished (smaller than the object). This occurs because concave lenses diverge light rays, making them appear to come from a point closer to the lens than the actual object position. Option 1 is correct because concave lenses always produce diminished images for real objects. Option 2 (point size) is incorrect—this only happens when the object is at infinity. Option 3 (same size) is incorrect—concave lenses cannot produce same-sized images for real objects. Option 4 (enlarged) is incorrect— concave lenses never magnify; only convex lenses can produce enlarged images under certain conditions.
qs.kf:
☛ Concave lenses are also called diverging lenses because they spread out light rays.
☛ They are used in devices like peepholes, eyeglasses for myopia (nearsightedness), and some telescope eyepieces.
☛ The image formed by a concave lens is always virtual, erect, and diminished regardless of object position (except when object is at infinity, giving a point-sized image at focus).
☛ Focal length (f) of a concave lens is measured as negative in the Cartesian sign convention used in optics.
☛ Magnification (m) for concave lenses is always less than 1 for real objects, meaning the image is smaller than the object. Important One-liners for Upcoming Exams:

☛ What is the sign of focal length for a concave lens? → Negative
☛ Which lens is used to correct myopia? → Concave lens
☛ What is the magnification value range for a concave lens with real object? → 0 < |m| < 1

q: In the treatment of cancer, which of the following is used in external radiation therapy?
qs.e: In external radiation therapy for cancer treatment, Cobalt-60 (60 Co) is used as a radioisotope source in teletherapy machines. It emits gamma rays (γ-rays) with energies of 1.17 MeV and 1.33 MeV, which penetrate deep into tissues to destroy cancer cells. Cobalt-60 has a half-life of 5.27 years, making it suitable for medical use. Iodine-131 is used internally for thyroid cancer treatment via ingestion. Plutonium-238 is used in radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) for space missions, not medical therapy. Hydrogen-3 (Tritium) is a low-energy beta emitter used in research and luminous paints, not for external radiation therapy.

q: How is the acceleration due to gravity denoted?
qs.e: In physics and chemistry, the acceleration due to gravity is denoted by the lowercase letter g. This represents the acceleration experienced by objects in a gravitational field, typically near Earth's surface, with a standard value of approximately 9.8 m/s². Greek letters are not used for this notation: there is no "Greek letter g" in standard physics notation, and epsilon (ε) represents other quantities like permittivity or strain. q: Who discovered the electron?

q: Name the British chemist who presented his atomic theory in 1808, on conservation of mass and law of definite proportions, which was a turning point in the study of matter.
qs.e: The correct answer is John Dalton, a British chemist who proposed his atomic theory in 1808. Dalton's theory was based on the law of conservation of mass (mass is neither created nor destroyed in chemical reactions) and the law of definite proportions (a chemical compound always contains exactly the same proportion of elements by mass). His theory stated that all matter is composed of indivisible atoms, atoms of the same element are identical, and compounds form from combinations of atoms in simple whole-number ratios. This was revolutionary as it provided a quantitative foundation for chemistry. Ernest Rutherford (option 1) discovered the atomic nucleus in 1911, much later. Lavoisier (option 2) formulated the law of conservation of mass in 1789 but did not propose an atomic theory. Proust (option 3) established the law of definite proportions in 1794 but also did not develop a comprehensive atomic model.

q: The process wherein the body of the living organism splits into two exactly identical halves is termed as ___________.
qs.e: This question relates to reproduction in living organisms, specifically asexual reproduction methods. Binary fission is the process where a single organism divides into two genetically identical daughter cells. This occurs in unicellular organisms like bacteria (e.g., Escherichia coli) and some protists (e.g., Amoeba). The parent cell's DNA replicates, and the cell splits into two equal halves. Budding (Option 1) involves a small outgrowth forming a new individual, as in yeast. Fragmentation (Option 2) is when the body breaks into pieces, each growing into a new organism, seen in planaria. Multiple fission (Option 4) produces many daughter cells simultaneously, as in Plasmodium (malaria parasite). Binary fission is correct because it specifically describes splitting into two identical halves.

☛ In Amoeba, binary fission is irregular, while in Leishmania (cause of kala-azar), it is longitudinal.
☛ Budding is seen in Hydra and yeast, where a bud detaches to form a new individual.
☛ Fragmentation occurs in spirogyra (algae) and flatworms, where each fragment regenerates.
☛ Multiple fission is observed in Plasmodium during its life cycle, producing many merozoites. Important One-liners for Upcoming Exams:
